headline: The Macintosh
text: Apple presented the Macintosh on 24 January, two days after a 1.5 million dollar television commercial by the film director Ridley Scott ran during the Super Bowl. The Mac is worked with a mouse and pictures on the screen, has a 9-inch screen and 128 kilobytes of memory, and costs 2,495 dollars. The commercial, seen by some 43 million Americans, shows a young woman smashing the screen of a 'Big Brother' who stands for IBM.
imageCaption: Steve Jobs with the Macintosh, January 1984

headline: Nestlé agrees to follow the baby-milk code; US boycott suspended
text: After talks with the boycott groups, Nestlé has agreed to implement the World Health Organization's code on selling breast-milk substitutes and to set up an independent audit commission. In return the boycott, which began in the United States in July 1977, is being called off.
imageCaption: Nestlé's headquarters on Lake Geneva in Vevey, 1963
imageCredit: Robert Cutts from Bristol, England, UK

headline: Diet Coke takes off
text: Coca-Cola's net income rose 9% to 559 million dollars in 1983 on revenue of 6.8 billion. Diet Coke, launched only in July 1982, captured 17% of the fast-growing US diet soft drink market by the end of 1983 and became the fourth best-selling soft drink in North America; it has been introduced in 28 markets abroad. Coca-Cola products make up more than 35% of the soft drinks drunk worldwide.

headline: Disney shares soar on takeover buying
text: Disney shares jumped in March amid heavy buying and talk of a takeover. The financier Saul Steinberg began buying the stock on 12 March, at about 50 dollars a share, attracted by Disney's land, film library and low share price compared with the value of its assets.

headline: Sam Walton dances the hula on Wall Street
text: On 15 March Wal-Mart's chairman Sam Walton, 65, danced the hula in front of Merrill Lynch on Wall Street with a Hawaiian band, keeping a promise to his employees. He had bet they could not lift the company's pre-tax profit to 8% of sales in 1983. They did.
imageCaption: Sam Walton dances the hula on Wall Street in a grass skirt and leis, New York, 15 March 1984

headline: Intel's first billion-dollar year
text: Intel's annual report for 1983 shows sales up 25 percent to more than one billion dollars, the first time it has passed that mark, after two difficult years. Chairman Gordon Moore wrote: "We closed 1983 with a bang." The economic recovery has brought strong demand for chips for personal computers and factory automation.
imageCaption: Gordon Moore, Intel's co-founder and chairman, 1978

headline: 'Apple II Forever': a portable Apple, and the shares jump 27 percent
text: Three months after the Macintosh, Apple showed on 24 April that it is not giving up the computer that made it big. At an event called 'Apple II Forever' it presented the Apple IIc, a small Apple II that weighs 3.4 kilograms, has the disk drive built in and can be carried from room to room. It costs 1,295 dollars, about half as much as a Macintosh, and Apple wants to sell 400,000 of them this year. The shares gained 27 percent in April.
imageCaption: The Apple IIc with its small monitor, 1984

headline: Swiss voters keep bank secrecy
text: On 20 May Swiss voters rejected the popular initiative 'against the abuse of bank client confidentiality and bank power' by 73% to 27%; not a single canton approved it. Turnout was about 42.5%. The big banks can go on guarding their clients' secrets as before.
imageCaption: The Paradeplatz in Zurich with the Bankverein (left) and the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt (right), 1971

headline: Disney pays the raider to go away
text: Disney agreed to buy back Saul Steinberg's 4.2 million shares at 70.83 dollars each, 297.4 million dollars, plus 28 million for his expenses, giving him a profit of about 32 million dollars. He had offered to buy 37.9% of the company at 67.50 dollars a share. After the deal Disney's stock fell nearly 16 dollars to 49.50 in five trading days, and shareholders sued. Paying a raider to leave is called greenmail.

headline: A bond rally lifts shares 11 percent in August
text: Interest rates fell sharply over the summer, with yields on bonds down about 5/8 to 3/4 of a percentage point since mid-July, as the economy's expansion turned out slower than expected. Shares jumped with bonds: the S&P 500 rose 11% in August to 166.68. Earlier in the summer the Fed chairman, Paul Volcker, and the head of the SEC, John Shad, warned about the mountains of debt being piled up in takeovers.
imageCaption: President Reagan gives his acceptance speech at the Republican convention, Dallas, 23 August 1984

headline: Nestlé agrees to buy Carnation for $3 billion
text: On 4 September Nestlé agreed to buy the American food company Carnation for $83 a share in cash, about $3 billion, with the board's support; it is buying the 27% held by the founder's descendants first. Carnation, with 1983 sales of $3.4 billion and 22,000 employees, makes evaporated milk, Coffee-Mate creamer and Friskies pet food. Carnation shares rose $4 to $79.50 in New York.

headline: Schlumberger buys the offshore driller Sedco
text: Sedco, an offshore drilling company, agreed in September to merge with Schlumberger, a deal valued at about 1 billion dollars. It adds drilling rigs at sea to Schlumberger's business of measuring what lies underground, next to its own drilling arm, Forex Neptune.

headline: Indira Gandhi is assassinated
text: On 31 October India's prime minister Indira Gandhi was shot dead at her home in New Delhi by two of her own bodyguards. They were Sikhs taking revenge: in June she had sent the army into the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the holiest place of the Sikh religion, to drive out armed militants. Her son Rajiv Gandhi has been sworn in as prime minister.

headline: Reagan re-elected in a 49-state landslide
text: On 6 November Ronald Reagan, 73, won a second term with 525 of 538 electoral votes and 58.8% of the popular vote; Walter Mondale carried only his home state of Minnesota and the District of Columbia. Mondale had made history by choosing Geraldine Ferraro as his running mate, the first woman on a major party ticket. With inflation down to about 4% and the economy growing fast, "Morning in America" was an easy sell.
imageCaption: President Reagan and Nancy Reagan receive Walter Mondale's concession call, Los Angeles, 6 November 1984

headline: 1984 in review: a flat year as rates rise and fall
text: The S&P 500 ended 1984 at 167.24, up only 1%, and the Dow fell 3.7% to 1,211.57. Interest rates rose in the first half, with the prime rate peaking at 13 percent in June, then fell back to 10.75 percent by 19 December. Shares are roughly where they were at the end of 1983.
imageCaption: American shares (S&P 500) at the end of each month of 1984: up 1 percent in the year
